lessons.still: Think of someone who often makes you impatient. Which of their habits gets to you most easily? Quietly ask the Lord to show you what weakness, hurt or limitation might lie behind it. Then consider the ways in which others need to be patient with you.
teach: When a family goes hiking together, there is always someone who walks slowly. The strong ones can complain, they can go on ahead, or they can slow down and take that person's backpack. Churches and families are hiking parties like this. Patient people don't leave the slow ones behind; they walk with them all the way to the summit.

Paul urges the Ephesians to bear “with one another in love”, and the word “bear with” carries the sense of “holding up under” or “carrying”. In Romans he says the strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, “and not to please ourselves.” Patience often has a cost: giving up our own efficiency, preferences and convenience to match someone else's pace.

Notice that Paul puts humility, gentleness and patience together. We are impatient with others often because deep down we think, “I'm better than they are.” The mindset shift: from “Why are they so slow?” to “I have weaknesses too, and the Lord has been carrying me all along.” The fruit of patience grows in the soil of humility.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to our place. Impatience is a sign of the self-ruled life: my time and my standards matter most. The self-emptied person does not seek to please themselves and gladly slows down. People matter more than tasks; never hurt people for the sake of efficiency.
q: Who is God? — How many of your weaknesses has God carried? As you think about this, what do you feel toward God?
Who am I? — With whom are you least patient? Is “I'm better than they are” hiding behind it?
How shall I respond? — How will you “slow down” for someone today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “won't break a bruised reed, and won't quench a smoking flax” (Matthew 12:20). He was always gentle and patient with the weak: patiently explaining things to slow-to-understand disciples, and holding out his nail-scarred hands to doubting Thomas.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for carrying my weaknesses all along and never rejecting me. I confess that I am often impatient with people and secretly think I am better than they are. Give me a humble, gentle and patient heart, to bear with others in love and not to please myself. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down one way others need to be patient with you
Today, take someone's “backpack” and walk a stretch with them
For one of my 2s: in the thing about them that tries your patience most, hold back from criticising
lessons.noon: “Bearing with one another in love” — Lord, right now let me slow down for them.

lessons.title: Practising Patience with My 2
lessons.theme: Let patience finish its work, so that we may be mature and complete

v: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations,
knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.
Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.
We exhort you, brothers: Admonish the disorderly; encourage the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient toward all.

lessons.still: Open your “My 2 List” and ask the Holy Spirit to show you whom you most need to be patient with this week. Picture that person standing before you, and say to the Lord, “Lord, this is the 2 you have given me. Through them, please complete your work of patience in me.”
teach: A diamond is formed when carbon spends a long time deep underground under great pressure and heat; without those years, carbon remains just carbon. James says, “Let endurance have its perfect work,” meaning let patience finish its job instead of breaking off halfway. The 2 who tests you most may be the very tool God is using to make you “perfect and complete”.

James says to “count it all joy” when we face trials, not because the trials themselves are pleasant, but because we know that trials produce endurance and endurance makes us mature. Paul in 1 Thessalonians 5:14 is more specific: different people call for different approaches (warning, encouraging, supporting), but we are to be patient with everyone. Patience is not doing nothing; it is loving persistently in the right way.

This week we have seen God's long-suffering patience, the endurance of Job, waiting for God's time, and bearing with others' weaknesses. Now practise patience concretely with one of your 2s. We have come through love, joy, peace and patience; next week we will learn a warmer fruit that grows within patience: kindness.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Among the eight steps for changing our mindset, “Repetition” is the training ground of patience: practising, reviewing, correcting and practising again, time after time. The fruit of patience is not self-cultivation; it is the life of Christ flowing out of a self-emptied person. Let Jesus reign in our trials, making us perfect and complete.
q: Who is God? — God lets trials produce endurance. What are his intentions for your growth?
Who am I? — With your 2, at what moment are you most likely to give up on patience?
How shall I respond? — This week, will you love your 2 patiently by warning, encouraging or supporting them?
lessons.jesus: For three years Jesus walked with his disciples. Again and again they argued about who was the greatest, and again and again they misunderstood his mission. Yet even at the Last Supper Jesus still stooped to wash their feet. “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” This is the love that lets patience finish its work.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you loved me to the end and never gave up halfway. Let patience finish its work in me, so that I may be perfect and complete. As I face my 2 this week, give me wisdom to know when to warn, when to encourage and when to support, and to be patient always. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: For one of my 2s: this week, deliberately give them more time in one matter
Memorise this week's verse: James 1:4
Write down one moment this week when you experienced the fruit of patience
lessons.noon: “Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete.” — Lord, right now complete your work of patience in me.

mem.t: And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.title: God's Kindness Leads to Repentance
lessons.theme: It isn't scolding that brings us back; it is kindness that leads us home

v: Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?
But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared,
not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,

lessons.still: Quietly reflect: did you turn back to God because you were scolded, or because you were treated with kindness? Let a picture of God's kindness to you come to mind. Stay there, and say to the Lord, “It was your kindness that led me home.”
teach: The North Wind and the Sun made a bet over which of them could make a traveller take off his coat. The harder the North Wind blew, the more tightly the traveller wrapped his coat around himself; but when the Sun shone warmly, he took the coat off of his own accord. The fable expresses a spiritual principle: harshness makes people defensive, while warmth makes them open up.

Paul says God's kindness “leads you to repentance.” The word “leads” is like a shepherd leading his sheep, gentle yet firm. Titus says God saved us not because of righteous things we had done, but according to his mercy, when “the kindness of God our Savior” appeared. Repentance doesn't come from being scolded awake; it comes from being melted by love.

The original word for kindness carries the sense of being useful, fitting and gentle toward others; it is goodness with warmth, actively given. When we want to change other people, we often use the North Wind's method: criticism, blame and pressure. The mindset shift: God changed me through kindness, so I too will treat my 2 with kindness and let God's warmth melt hearts.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled person tries to change others by force, provoking pride so that both sides lose; the self-emptied person opens hearts with kindness, and humility inspires humility. The fruit of kindness is not self-cultivation; it is God's kindness in Christ shining naturally out of a self-emptied person.
q: Who is God? — God leads you to repentance with kindness rather than scolding. What kind of God does this show you?
Who am I? — When you want to change someone, do you more often act like the North Wind or the Sun?
How shall I respond? — What act of kindness will you put in place of a criticism today?
lessons.jesus: Zacchaeus climbed a tree to watch the spectacle, perhaps also braced for people's pointing fingers. But Jesus stopped and called him by name: “Today I must stay at your house.” Not a word of rebuke, yet Zacchaeus repented on the spot. Jesus' kindness was more powerful than any condemnation.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for leading me to repentance with kindness, and for saving me not by my righteousness but by your mercy. I confess that I often try to change others with criticism and pressure. Make me like you, melting hearts with the warmth of kindness, so that people taste your grace through me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down a time when God's kindness turned you back
Today, replace one criticism you want to make with an act of kindness
For one of my 2s: show your goodwill toward them in some small way
lessons.noon: “Not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?” — Lord, right now let me be warm toward people, like the sun.

lessons.title: David's Kindness to Mephibosheth
lessons.theme: Kindness actively seeks out those who cannot repay

v: David said, “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”

David said to him, “Don’t be afraid, for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and will restore to you all the land of Saul your father. You will eat bread at my table continually.”

lessons.still: Imagine yourself as Mephibosheth: lame in both feet, living in remote Lo Debar, summoned before the king and bowing down in fear. Then hear the king say, “Don't be afraid.” Quietly let these words become the Lord's words to you.
teach: In the ancient world, a new king would often wipe out the descendants of the previous royal house to prevent future trouble. David did the opposite. He took the initiative to ask, “Is there anyone left of the house of Saul?” not to destroy them but to show them kindness. The question itself is where kindness begins: kindness does not wait to be asked; it goes looking.

Mephibosheth was lame in both feet and a descendant of David's old enemy; he was of no use to David and might even be a threat. Yet because of the covenant he had made with Jonathan, David showed him kindness: he restored his lands and let him eat at the king's table continually. Mephibosheth's response was, “What is your servant, that you should look at such a dead dog as I am?” Kindness shines most brightly when it reaches the undeserving.

Each of us is a spiritual Mephibosheth: crippled by sin, yet invited to the King's banquet because of the covenant God made in Christ. The mindset shift: I show kindness to people not because they deserve it, but because I was shown kindness first. Today, is there someone around you, someone “left of the house of Saul”, waiting to be shown kindness?
lessons.light: 321 Light: David laid down a king's power. He did not use it for revenge but for kindness, and this is the authority of the self-emptied life. Those who let Jesus reign will use everything in their hands to bless others. Kindness is the overflow of Christ's life, not the product of self-cultivation.
q: Who is God? — Like David, God takes the initiative to seek you out and invite you to his table. How does that make you feel?
Who am I? — Are you kind only to those who are useful to you and can repay you?
How shall I respond? — Who around you is someone “left of the house of Saul”, needing you to go and show them kindness?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “When you make a dinner or a supper, don't call your friends… But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind; and you will be blessed” (Luke 14:12–14). He himself did exactly that, eating with tax collectors and sinners.
lessons.pray: Lord, I am that lame Mephibosheth, yet for Christ's sake you have invited me to your table. Thank you for seeking me out. Help me too to seek out those who cannot repay me, and to use all that you have given me to show them kindness, for your glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Read 2 Samuel 9, noticing each of David's acts of kindness
Invite someone who is often overlooked for a cup of tea or a meal
For one of my 2s: take the initiative to do something for them that they cannot repay
lessons.noon: “You will eat bread at my table continually.” — Lord, right now I sit at the banquet of your grace.

lessons.title: Clothed with Kindness
lessons.theme: Kindness is not a single act but a heart we put on

v: Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;
bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
“Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful.

lessons.still: As you get dressed this morning, notice yourself putting on each item of clothing. Then, in your heart, “put on” these one by one as well: compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience. Say to the Lord, “Lord, today I go out wearing your heart.”
teach: We get dressed every morning; nobody skips it because they wore clothes yesterday. Paul says we are to have “a heart of compassion, kindness…”, and the word he uses means to “put on”. Kindness is not an occasional good deed; it is clothing we put on every morning, so that when people see us they see the likeness of Christ.

Paul first states who we are, “God's chosen ones, holy and beloved,” and only then says what to put on. We don't put on kindness in order to be loved; we put on kindness because we are already loved. Jesus also said: be merciful, just as your Father is merciful. Kindness is the family likeness; children resemble their Father.

Paul specifically mentions “if anyone has a complaint against another.” Kindness is tested most in relationships where there is friction. The mindset shift: kindness doesn't depend on my mood or on who the other person is; it depends on who I am. I am beloved, so I choose to put on a kind heart every day, even toward someone I have friction with.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Putting on the new self means taking off the old, self-ruled self. The five qualities Paul lists here (compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience) are the very pattern of the self-emptied life. The focus is on Jesus, not on whether the other person deserves it. Kindness is the natural overflow of Christ's life in a self-emptied person.
q: Who is God? — “Holy and beloved”: this is what God calls you. Do you believe it?
Who am I? — Does your kindness depend on your mood or on who the other person is?
How shall I respond? — How will you remind yourself to “put on” a kind heart today?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus saw a widow at the funeral of her only son, he “had compassion on her, and said to her, ‘Don't cry,’” and then raised her son to life. No one asked him; he stopped of his own accord. Kindness was not an occasional act for him; it was the heart he always wore.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for calling me holy and beloved. Today I will put on a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Make me merciful as you are merciful, so that even with those I have friction with I can bear with them and forgive them, just as you forgave me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: As you get dressed this morning, pray silently, “I put on kindness”
Show a small kindness to someone you have friction with
For one of my 2s: today, answer everything they say in a gentle tone
lessons.noon: “Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful.” — Lord, right now I put on your kindness.

lessons.title: Kindness in Our Words
lessons.theme: A word that builds others up is the most common fruit of kindness

v: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

lessons.still: Think back over what you said yesterday. Which words did someone good? Which might have hurt someone? Don't beat yourself up; just bring it honestly before the Lord. Then ask him to guard your mouth today so that your words carry kindness.
teach: It's easy to squeeze toothpaste out of the tube, but almost impossible to put it back. Words are the same: once spoken, they cannot be taken back. We may not do many great things in a day, but we say thousands of words. Our speech is the most everyday place for the fruit of kindness, and also the place where it is most easily seen, or where we most easily wound.

Paul says to speak “only what is good for building others up.” “Building up” is originally a construction word. Every word is a brick: it can build a wall, or it can tear a house down. Proverbs says, “A gentle answer turns away wrath.” Say the same thing gently and anger subsides; say it harshly and anger flares up.

Kindness in our words does not mean saying only nice things and never the truth; it means speaking the truth in love, choosing a time and a way that builds others up. The mindset shift: before speaking, ask three questions. Is it true? Is it necessary? Will it build up? Let the Holy Spirit be Lord before we open our mouths.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Out of the heart flow the springs of life, and our words also pour out from the heart. The self-ruled person speaks to prove themselves and win; the self-emptied person speaks to build others up and glorify God. Speaking from the heart by the Spirit means letting Jesus reign over our tongues.
q: Who is God? — God created all things by his word. What power does his word have for you?
Who am I? — In what situations do you most often speak harshly?
How shall I respond? — To whom will you speak a word that builds them up today?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus preached in the synagogue at Nazareth, “all testified about him, and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth” (Luke 4:22). To the woman caught in adultery he said, “Neither do I condemn you”; to Peter he said, “Feed my sheep.” Every word he spoke was full of grace and truth.
lessons.pray: Lord, guard my mouth so that today I speak no corrupt words, only words that build others up. When I want to hit back, help me give a gentle answer that turns away wrath. Let your gracious words flow from my mouth, giving grace to those who hear. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Before you speak, ask: Is it true? Is it necessary? Will it build up?
Today, take the initiative to praise a specific strength in someone
For one of my 2s: send them a message of encouragement
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath.” — Lord, right now guard my mouth.

lessons.title: Showing Kindness to My 2
lessons.theme: Be kind to one another, just as God in Christ forgave me

v: Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.still: Open your “My 2 List” and ask the Holy Spirit to show you whom you are to show kindness to this week. If you still hold bitterness or resentment toward them, first hand it honestly to the Lord. Then think of how the Lord has been kind to you, and carry that kindness to that person.
teach: Before a gardener plants flowers, he must clear away the stones and weeds; otherwise even the best seed will not grow. Paul likewise speaks of putting off before putting on: first put away bitterness, wrath, anger, shouting, slander and malice, and then “be kind to one another.” The fruit of kindness cannot grow in a field of bitterness.

Ephesians 4:32 contains three actions: be kind to one another, be tender-hearted, forgive one another. The power for all of them lies in the final phrase: “just as God in Christ forgave you.” We don't show kindness on the strength of the other person's behaviour, but on the strength of the forgiveness of the cross. Those who have been forgiven much love much, and are kind in abundance.

This week we have seen God's kindness leading to repentance, David's kindness reaching out, putting on a kind heart, and kindness in our words. Now show kindness concretely to one of your 2s. Kindness is the warmth of goodness, and goodness is kindness in action; next week we will learn the next fruit, closely tied to kindness: goodness.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Building God's kingdom system begins with one act of forgiveness. Bitterness is the root of the self-ruled life: I want justice, I want to be the judge. Forgiveness is the fruit of the self-emptied life: handing judgement to God and returning to our place. Kindness is not self-cultivation; it is Christ's forgiveness flowing through us.
q: Who is God? — How much has God forgiven you in Christ? As you think about this, how do you respond?
Who am I? — Is there still bitterness in your heart blocking the growth of the fruit of kindness?
How shall I respond? — This week, toward which 2 will you show kindness, and with what concrete action?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus not only forgave those who crucified him; he also said to the repentant thief beside him, “Today you will be with me in Paradise.” In his moment of deepest pain, he was still kind, giving the hope of heaven to someone who did not deserve it.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that in Christ all my sins have been forgiven. I hand you the bitterness, resentment and anger in my heart; please take them away. This week I will be kind to one of my 2s, tender-hearted and forgiving, just as you forgave me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: For one of my 2s: do one concrete act of kindness this week
Write down one bitterness you need to let go of, and lay it at the foot of the cross
Memorise this week's verse: Ephesians 4:32
lessons.noon: “Just as God also in Christ forgave you.” — Lord, right now let your forgiveness flow through me to them.

mem.t: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.

lessons.title: Goodness Comes from God
lessons.theme: Goodness is not the polish of a good person but the overflow of God's nature

v: Oh taste and see that the LORD is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation nor turning shadow.

lessons.still: Sit comfortably with your open hands resting on your knees, as if receiving a gift. Slowly count your blessings: today's breath, the sunlight, your food, the people around you; all of it has come down from the Father of lights. Softly say, “Lord, you are good.”
teach: Whether well water tastes sweet doesn't depend on the bucket but on the source. We often think of “goodness” as a personal quality: being good-tempered, helpful, never harming anyone. But Jesus said, “No one is good except one: God.” Human goodness cut off from God is like a bucket cut off from its spring; before long it runs dry.

The psalmist invites us to “taste and see that the Lord is good,” because God's goodness is not a theory but something we can experience. James says every good and perfect gift is “from above,” from the Father “with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.” The sun sets, the moon waxes and wanes, human hearts change; only God's goodness never changes.

So the goodness the Spirit produces is not me trying hard to become a good person; it is the God who is good living in me, and his goodness flowing out through me. The mindset shift: from “I must be a good person” to “I must abide in the good God.” Get the source right, and the water will be sweet.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-ruled goodness usually comes with self-promotion: “I'm a good person.” Self-emptied goodness gives the glory to the source: “It is God's goodness in me.” Let Jesus reign and let Jesus receive all the glory, including the glory for our good deeds.
q: Who is God? — “With whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.” What qualities of God's goodness do you see here?
Who am I? — Does your “goodness” come from God, or do you prop it up by your own effort?
How shall I respond? — How will you “taste and see that the Lord is good” today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him” (Acts 10:38). His good deeds were not done to build a reputation; they were the Father's goodness flowing naturally through him. He said that by himself he could do nothing, but only what he saw the Father doing.
lessons.pray: Good and gracious God, thank you for every good gift you have given me. I confess that there is no goodness in me; whatever good there is comes from you. Be the source of my life, and let your goodness flow out of me, so that people see you and not me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down five good gifts you have received from God today
For one of my 2s: tell them one good thing God has given them
After doing a good deed, pray silently: “Glory to the God who is good.”
lessons.noon: “Oh taste and see that the LORD is good.” — Lord, right now let me taste your goodness.

lessons.title: Don't Grow Weary in Doing Good
lessons.theme: Sow to the Spirit, and in due season there will be a harvest

v: For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.

lessons.still: Imagine you are a farmer holding a handful of seed. Recall, one by one, the good things you have done lately that have brought no return, and place them in the Lord's hand like seed being sown, saying, “Lord, the time of harvest is yours.” Then breathe quietly, and let go of the anxious need to see results right away.
teach: A farmer who sows his seed doesn't dig up the soil the next day to see whether it has sprouted. While the seed is hidden underground, it is putting down roots. Doing good is like that: we give, and the other person doesn't say thank you, nothing changes, and we may even be misunderstood. At such times the greatest temptation is not to do evil but to “grow weary”: forget it, why bother?

Paul says there are two ways of sowing: sowing to the flesh and sowing to the Spirit. If we do good to win people's praise, we are sowing to the flesh, and when the applause stops we lose heart. If we do good by following the Spirit, we don't look at people's response but at God's timing. “In due season”: the harvest timetable is in God's hands, not ours.

“As we have opportunity, let us do good to all”: doing good is not an occasional burst of enthusiasm but a way of life. We grow weary usually because our focus has drifted to results or to other people. Turn the focus back to Jesus: I do good because he was good to me first, and he will never forget a single seed sown for his name.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on yourself, not on others, not on circumstances. Calculate the returns with your head and you will be full of worry; live from the heart by the Spirit and your heart will be glad. Shift your perspective from the temporary to the eternal: the harvest you cannot see today will not lose a single grain in eternity.
q: Who is God? — “We will reap in due season.” How do you trust the God who holds the seasons?
Who am I? — In which good work have you already begun to lose heart?
How shall I respond? — Where will you keep on “sowing to the Spirit” today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus spent his life doing good, and in return he was rejected, betrayed and crucified. From a human point of view it was the greatest “waste” of all; from God's point of view it was the greatest harvest. “For the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising its shame.” A grain of wheat fell into the ground and produced many seeds.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that after doing good for a long time I grow tired, and I long to be noticed. Renew my resolve, so that I no longer sow for people's applause but sow to the Spirit. I place the time of harvest in your hands; give me strength not to lose heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Keep on with one good work you nearly gave up on
For one of my 2s: keep up a kind gesture toward them without expecting anything in return
Write “The time of harvest is in God's hands” and put it where you will often see it
lessons.noon: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.” — Lord, right now strengthen my heart.

lessons.title: The Good Works of Dorcas
lessons.theme: The good works God prepared are shown through ordinary hands

v: Peter got up and went with them. When he had come, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the tunics and other garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.

lessons.still: Look at your hands. Today they may type on a keyboard, cook a meal, hold a child or sweep the floor. Lift them up and offer them to the Lord: “Lord, these hands are yours; please use them.” Be silent for a moment, and ask the Lord to show you one need around you.
teach: Dorcas never preached a sermon or performed a miracle. Scripture records only that she was “full of good works and acts of mercy”. When she died, the widows gathered around Peter weeping, and what they held in their hands was not her sermons but the tunics and garments she had sewn herself. Every stitch was her testimony left behind on earth.

Paul says, “We are his workmanship.” The word carries the sense of a masterpiece, a work of art. God has re-created us in Christ “for good works”, and these good works are ones “which God prepared beforehand” for us. It is like a road already laid down; we simply obey and walk on it. Good works are not something we dream up to prove ourselves; they are what God has placed on our path ahead of time.

We often think only big things count as serving, but Dorcas's needle and thread tell us that in God's eyes nothing is small. The fruit of goodness often grows in the most ordinary places: a meal, a garment, a phone call. The mindset shift: not “I must do something remarkable,” but “What good work has God prepared for me today?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied person needs no stage, because they do not live for their own name. Dorcas's good works let the widows see God's love, and later many came to believe in the Lord because of what happened. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: a good life naturally builds relationships, and relationships naturally become bridges for the gospel.
q: Who is God? — God has “prepared” good works for you. What kind of God does this show you?
Who am I? — What ordinary things do you have in your hands that could become God's “needle and thread”?
How shall I respond? — What good work has God placed on your path today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus took a boy's five loaves and two fish, gave thanks, broke them and handed them to the disciples, and five thousand were fed. He did not despise a small lunch. He also stooped to wash his disciples' feet: the Lord of the universe displayed God's goodness with a towel and a basin of water.
lessons.pray: Lord my Creator, thank you for calling me your workmanship and for preparing good works for me to do. Open my eyes to see the people you have placed on my path, and use my ordinary hands, as you used Dorcas's, to pass on your love stitch by stitch. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Prepare a small, practical help for someone in need around you
For one of my 2s: do one concrete act of service, such as bringing a meal or writing a card
In the evening, reflect: “Did I do the good work God prepared for me today?”
lessons.noon: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” — Lord, right now let me see the good work you have prepared.

lessons.title: Overcoming Evil with Good
lessons.theme: Evil cannot be defeated by evil, only overcome by good

v: Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
not rendering evil for evil or insult for insult; but instead blessing, knowing that you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing.

lessons.still: Think of someone who has hurt you and made you want to hit back. Don't suppress your feelings; tell the Lord honestly, “Lord, I am hurt.” Then breathe deeply, lay your thoughts of revenge like stones at the foot of the cross, and ask the Lord to give you a heart that blesses.
teach: Fight fire with fire and the blaze only grows; only water puts it out. When we are treated badly, our instinct is to repay evil with evil: you're cold to me, so I'll be cold to you; you say one thing to me, I'll say two back. The evil snowballs and both sides lose. This is exactly how pride provokes pride.

Paul says, “Don't be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” Repaying evil with evil looks like fighting back, but in fact it means evil has won: it has succeeded in turning me into an evildoer too. Peter goes further: “but instead blessing,” because “you were called to this.” Blessing our enemies is not weakness; it is a heavenly victory.

Overcoming evil with good does not mean swallowing our anger and pretending nothing happened; it means refusing to let evil decide how I respond. I can set boundaries and speak the truth, yet without holding a grudge or taking revenge, leaving vengeance to God. The key is: who is reigning right now? If self is on the throne, I will want to settle the score; if Jesus is on the throne, I can bless the other person.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility overcomes pride; the self-emptied life overcomes Satan. What Satan wants most is to get us repaying evil for evil, trapped in the cycle of the self-ruled life. Humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Overcoming evil with good is exactly how the vicious cycle is broken and God's kingdom system is built.
q: Who is God? — God was good to us while we were still his enemies. What does this teach you about him?
Who am I? — Is there a debt in your heart that you want to “collect”?
How shall I respond? — What specific good can you return for an evil today?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was insulted, he did not answer back; as he was being crucified, he prayed for those who nailed him there: “Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing.” The cross looked like the triumph of evil, but it was in fact the ultimate victory of good. He absorbed all evil with love, and overcame it all.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, on the cross you overcame evil with good. I confess that I often want to repay evil with evil and settle the score. Today I hand my right to vengeance over to you. Keep me from being overcome by evil, and enable me instead to bless those who have hurt me. Reign in my heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Pray a prayer of blessing for someone who has hurt you
For one of my 2s: when there's friction, hold back from hitting back and say something kind instead
When you are offended today, pray silently: “Don't be overcome by evil.”
lessons.noon: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” — Lord, right now help me respond with good.

lessons.title: Doing Good to My 2
lessons.theme: Let good works be a light that shines on those around us

v: Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
But don’t forget to be doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.

lessons.still: In your heart, list three of “my 2s”: family, colleagues, neighbours or brothers and sisters in Christ. Pause quietly over each name, asking the Lord to show you what they need right now, and how you can be a blessing to them.
teach: A lamp doesn't need to announce loudly, “I'm shining!” Once it is lit, the room is simply filled with light. This week we have seen that the source of goodness is God (Day 1), that we must not grow weary in doing good (Day 2), that we do the good God has prepared in ordinary ways (Day 3), and that we overcome evil with good (Day 4). Today we bring goodness to the people closest to us: our 2s.

Jesus said to let people “see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” Notice the direction of the glory: it goes not to the one doing good but to the Father in heaven. Hebrews says doing good and sharing are sacrifices that please God; our good deeds are themselves an act of worship offered to God.

Doing good to “my 2s” is hardest, because they know us best and rub up against us most often. But for that very reason, our goodness is most real in front of them. Next week we will learn “faithfulness”, and faithfulness is exactly the strength that makes goodness last: not being good to people now and then, but being reliably good to them over the long haul.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The practice of 920: every person I am in relationship with is my 2; I live out the 0 of the self-emptied life; and the 9, the fruit of the Spirit, grows. Goodness is not done to be seen but so that the Father is glorified. Letting Jesus receive all the glory is the final direction of every good deed.
q: Who is God? — God is pleased with the sacrifice of doing good. What does this show you about what God values?
Who am I? — In the eyes of your 2s, are you a steady lamp or one that flickers on and off?
How shall I respond? — This week, toward which 2 will you keep doing one good thing?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was most patient in doing good to his closest disciples: when Peter was weak, he prayed for Peter; when Thomas doubted, he held out his hands; when the disciples argued about who was the greatest, he washed their feet. His light was not a distant searchlight but a lamp close at hand, lighting up the people beside him day after day.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for making me the light of the world. I place my 2s in your hands one by one. Help me show them your goodness, not for my own name but only for your glory. May they see not me, but you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: For one of my 2s: do one concrete good deed for them, and don't mention it
Write a one-line prayer for each of three 2s, and pray for them every day for a week
Tomorrow (Saturday), share with a spiritual companion how you did good this week
lessons.noon: “That they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” — Lord, right now let my light shine out your glory.

mem.t: Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.

lessons.title: The Faithfulness of God
lessons.theme: God’s faithfulness is new every morning; he never breaks his word

v: It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.
They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself.”

lessons.still: Look out of the window at the sky, and remember that this morning the sun rose just as it always does. Quietly say, “Lord, great is your faithfulness.” Then recall three moments in the past year when God did not abandon you, and thank him for each one in turn.
teach: The sunrise is never late, and it never needs us to remind it. When Jeremiah wrote Lamentations, Jerusalem had just been burned and the temple lay in ruins. Yet there, among the rubble, he wrote: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” His world had collapsed, but God had not.

Faithfulness here means that God keeps his word and keeps his covenant. Paul goes further: “If we are faithless, he remains faithful.” God’s faithfulness does not rest on our performance but on his own nature — “he can’t deny himself.” Our faithfulness runs hot and cold; his stands like a rock.

In the original language, the fruit of the Spirit called “faithfulness” is the same word as “faith.” We can be faithful to others because we have first experienced God’s faithfulness to us. A change of mindset: not “I must try hard to become a reliable person,” but “I stand on the God who is utterly reliable, and his faithfulness flows out through me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard — God’s word never fails, and it is the surest foundation for life. Self-ruled people trust only themselves, and so they are often let down by themselves; people living the self-emptied life lean on the faithful God, and so they become people others can lean on.
q: Who is God? — When you were at your lowest, how did God show you his faithfulness?
Who am I? — Do you assume that God’s faithfulness depends on how well you perform?
How shall I respond? — For which act of God’s faithfulness will you give thanks today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is called the one who is “Faithful and True” (Revelation 19:11). He said he would rise on the third day, and on the third day he rose from the dead; he promised to send the Counselor, and at Pentecost the Holy Spirit came. Peter denied him three times, yet Jesus held fast to his love and called Peter again by the lakeshore.
lessons.pray: Faithful God, thank you that your loving kindness never ends and your mercies are new every morning. Even when I am faithless, you remain faithful. Help me to live within your faithfulness, and let your faithfulness flow out through me, so that I become a blessing people can rely on. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down three things God has promised and faithfully done in your life
Tomorrow, make your first words on waking: “Lord, great is your faithfulness.”
Share with one of “my 2” a time when God was faithful to you
lessons.noon: “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” — Lord, right now I lean on your faithfulness.

lessons.title: Faithful in Little Things
lessons.theme: Faithfulness in big things begins with the smallest things

v: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.
If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?

lessons.still: List the small things you need to do today: reply to a message, arrive on time for an appointment, clear the dishes, finish a report. Place the list before the Lord and say, “Lord, in these small things too, I want to be faithful to you.”
teach: When a building collapses, it is often not because of one great earthquake but because, years earlier, a worker left out a few steel bars — “nobody will ever see it anyway.” Life is like that. Failure in big things usually grows out of compromise in small things, and faithfulness in big things is built up, little by little, in small things.

Jesus said, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” What God values is not the size of the task but the direction of the heart. We often think, “Once I have more time, more money, more influence, I’ll really use it for the Lord.” But Jesus says that if we have not been faithful in small matters like “unrighteous mammon,” who will entrust us with the “true riches”?

Small things are God’s training ground. Being on time, keeping your word, doing your own job well, never taking a cent that isn’t yours — these may seem trivial, but they are the foundations of character. A change of mindset: nothing is “too small to matter,” because everything is done before the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your mindset and you change your life; change your life and you change your lifestyle. The fruit of faithfulness is not produced on the platform but in the details of daily life. Letting Jesus reign includes letting him reign over every small thing I do.
q: Who is God? — God cares about even the smallest things — what does that show you about him?
Who am I? — In which “small things” do you often tell yourself, “This doesn’t matter”?
How shall I respond? — In which small thing will you be faithful to the Lord today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus spent many years as a carpenter in Nazareth, and Scripture records almost nothing of those years. Yet before he began his public ministry, the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” That pleasure included his ordinary, faithful days in the carpenter’s workshop.
lessons.pray: Lord, forgive me for so often despising small things and wanting only to do big ones. I am willing to be faithful to you in the smallest things: being on time, keeping my word, being honest, and doing well every task that is mine. In these ordinary days, produce in me the fruit of faithfulness. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Be on time for every appointment today; if you will be late, let people know in advance
Fulfil one small promise you have been putting off
Follow through for one of “my 2” on a small thing you once casually promised
lessons.noon: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” — Lord, right now I will be faithful to you in this small thing.

lessons.title: The Faithfulness of Daniel
lessons.theme: We stay faithful under pressure because our hearts already belong to God

v: Then the presidents and the local governors sought to find occasion against Daniel as touching the kingdom; but they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him.

When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.

lessons.still: Like Daniel, find a quiet corner. Kneel, or sit with your head bowed. Picture your window opening toward God’s presence. Don’t rush to speak; begin with thanks: “Lord, just as I always do, I come before you.”
teach: Only when the storm comes can you tell which tree has deep roots. Daniel served as an official in Babylon for decades, through more than one dynasty. His enemies wanted something to use against him and combed through all his affairs, yet “they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful.” In the end, the only place they could attack him was his faith.

Notice the words “as he did before.” When the decree was issued, Daniel didn’t change. He didn’t suddenly become brave; his everyday habit of praying three times a day had long since rooted his heart in God. His faithfulness at work and his faithfulness in prayer were two sides of one life: faithful to God, and therefore faithful to people.

When a crisis comes, we don’t suddenly rise to our ideals; we fall back to the level of our everyday habits. That is why today’s “as before” matters so much. Everyday prayer, everyday honesty, everyday diligence are the foundation that will let us stand firm in the future. Faithfulness is lived out one day at a time.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships — first with God, then with myself, then with others, then with things. Because Daniel’s relationship with God was secure, he could be faithful before people and in his work. His focus was on God, not on his circumstances, and not even a den of lions could change him.
q: Who is God? — God shut the lions’ mouths in the den — what does that show you about him?
Who am I? — What is your “as before”? When pressure comes, which habits will you fall back on?
How shall I respond? — Which “just as before” spiritual habit will you build?
lessons.jesus: On the night he faced the cross, Jesus still went out “as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives” to pray (Luke 22:39). His faithfulness was not a moment of heroism but the natural fruit of a lifetime of communion with the Father. On that darkest night he said, “Not my will, but yours, be done.”
lessons.pray: Lord, make me like Daniel, rooted in you in ordinary days. Whether at work, at home, or in church, let no one find grounds to charge me with unfaithfulness. When pressure comes, help me to stay faithful to you, just as I always have. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Set a regular daily time for prayer, and begin today
At work, do one task well that no one will ever check
Every day at a set time, pray for one of “my 2”
lessons.noon: “And prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.” — Lord, right now I come before you, just as I always do.

lessons.title: Entrusted According to Ability
lessons.theme: The Lord looks not at how much, but at faithfulness

v: “He also who got the two talents came and said, ‘Lord, you delivered to me two talents. Behold, I have gained another two talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things. I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’

lessons.still: Quietly ask yourself: what has the Lord entrusted to me? Time, health, skills, family, money, a job… Hold them one by one in the palm of your hand, the way a steward holds his master’s property, and say, “Lord, all of this is yours.”
teach: A steward lives in his master’s house and manages his master’s money, yet he knows full well that none of it is his. In the parable of the talents, the master entrusts different amounts “each according to his own ability”: one receives five talents, one two, one one. The amounts differ, but the responsibility is the same: faithfulness.

Notice that the servant with two talents receives exactly the same praise, word for word, as the one with five: “Well done, good and faithful servant.” The master does not grade on the size of the result but on faithfulness. The servant with one talent failed not because he received little but because he was afraid — he saw his master as a hard man, so he buried the money in the ground.

Wrong ideas about God make us afraid to take risks and unwilling to give. The fruit of faithfulness grows from a right knowledge of our Master: he is good, and he entrusts things to us because he trusts us. A change of mindset: from “I have only a little; it doesn’t matter” to “The Lord has given me this little, and I will be faithful with it.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: It is required of stewards that they be found faithful. Self-ruled people treat their gifts as their own assets — they either show them off or bury them. People living the self-emptied life know that everything belongs to the Lord, and they want only for their Master to receive the greatest glory. The glory is not mine; it belongs to Jesus.
q: Who is God? — The master gave both servants the same praise — what does that show you about God?
Who am I? — Because you feel you have “little ability,” have you buried your gifts?
How shall I respond? — Which talent the Lord has entrusted to you will you bring out and use today?
lessons.jesus: Before his suffering, Jesus prayed to the Father, “I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do” (John 17:4). He is the most faithful steward of all, completing every disciple and every task the Father entrusted to him. He kept nothing for himself, but gave all the glory to the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord, everything I have is entrusted to me by you. Forgive me for the times fear or comparison made me bury my gifts in the ground. I want to be your faithful steward, caring not about how much but about your pleasure. May I one day hear you say, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down five “talents” the Lord has entrusted to you
Bring out a gift you have long kept buried and use it to serve someone
Use one of your talents to give practical help to one of “my 2”
lessons.noon: “Well done, good and faithful servant.” — Lord, right now I choose to be faithful to you.

lessons.title: Keeping Faith with My 2
lessons.theme: Keeping your word is the most practical way to love

v: Many men claim to be men of unfailing love, but who can find a faithful man?
But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.

lessons.still: Think back over the past month. What did you promise, and to whom? Which promises did you keep, and which did you forget? Don’t beat yourself up; honestly hand the list to the Lord: “Lord, help me to keep my word.”
teach: No one dares to cross a bridge that is sometimes there and sometimes not. A relationship is a bridge too, and trust is its pillars. We say, “Let’s have a meal sometime,” “I’ll pray for you,” “Leave it to me” — and if nothing ever comes of it, the pillars are eaten away one by one. This week we have moved from God’s faithfulness (Day 1), to faithfulness in little things (Day 2), to Daniel (Day 3), to being entrusted according to our ability (Day 4), and now to today.

Solomon sighed, “Many men claim to be men of unfailing love, but who can find a faithful man?” Fine words are easy; keeping promises is hard. Jesus said, “Let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’” There is no need to swear oaths for emphasis, because a faithful person’s ordinary words are already worth trusting.

Keeping faith with my 2 means letting them experience God’s reliability through me. Keeping faith also includes explaining honestly when I can’t do something, rather than quietly disappearing. Next week we will learn about gentleness, and gentleness needs the soil of trust — only the gentleness of someone who keeps their word puts people at ease.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Breaking a promise may look like simply “forgetting something,” but in fact it wounds a person. The practice of 920 is to live out Christ’s faithfulness before each of my 2, so that our relationships become a witness to God’s kingdom.
q: Who is God? — God never breaks his word — what kind of security does that give you?
Who am I? — In the eyes of your 2, are you someone who keeps their word?
How shall I respond? — Which promise do you need to keep — or honestly explain — today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus told his disciples, “If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will receive you to myself.” He never promised lightly, and he never failed to keep a promise. His “Yes” is always “Yes”; all God’s promises are “Yes” in him (2 Corinthians 1:20).
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, you have never once broken faith with me. Forgive me for so often promising lightly and forgetting easily. Help me to keep my word to the people around me, letting my yes be yes and my no be no. May my 2 experience your faithfulness through me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Keep a promise you have been delaying for one of “my 2,” or honestly explain that you can’t
Don’t agree to things lightly today; when you do agree, write it down at once
Tomorrow (Saturday), share this week’s lessons in faithfulness with your spiritual companion
lessons.noon: “But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.” — Lord, right now make my words as reliable as yours.

mem.t: Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.

lessons.title: Jesus, Gentle and Humble in Heart
lessons.theme: Gentleness is not weakness; it is having power and refusing to use it to crush others

v: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

lessons.still: Relax your shoulders and notice the burdens you are carrying: work, family, relationships, worries. Breathe out slowly and picture yourself setting them down and taking up the Lord’s easy yoke instead. Softly say, “Lord, I come to learn from you.”
teach: A horse that has been broken in has lost none of its strength; it simply no longer charges about wildly, but responds to its master’s reins. In biblical times, Greek often used the word for “gentleness” to describe this kind of tamed strength. Gentleness is not a lack of strength; it is strength placed in God’s hands.

When Jesus described himself, he did not say, “I am mighty in heart,” but “I am gentle and humble in heart.” A yoke is carried by two oxen together, and Jesus invites us to share his yoke — he walks beside us, bears the weight, and sets our pace. To learn from him is to learn his gentle and humble heart.

This week we are learning the fruit of gentleness. Gentleness is not a naturally easygoing temperament. It belongs to a person who has accepted their place before God and so has no need to protect themselves by being hard. A change of mindset: gentleness is not losing; it is a strength only a heart at rest can have.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example. Humility is laying down power and returning to our place; gentleness is what humility looks like in our relationships. Self-ruled people use their strength to control others; people living the self-emptied life hand their strength to God, so they can treat others gently and find rest for their own souls.
q: Who is God? — The almighty Lord says, “I am gentle and humble in heart” — what does that show you about God?
Who am I? — Do you use your “strength” (your words, position, or knowledge) to push people down or to lift them up?
How shall I respond? — In which relationship will you learn from Jesus today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey’s colt — a king who came not on a warhorse but on a colt. He had authority to calm storms and drive out unclean spirits, yet he took little children in his arms and touched lepers; a bruised reed he would not break. His gentleness is the gentleness of the Almighty.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, gentle and humble, I lay down my burdens and come to you. I am willing to take your yoke and learn from you. Tame the hasty, hard self within me, and keep all my strength in your hands, to be used for lifting people up and never for pressing them down. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Memorise this week’s verse: Matthew 11:29
When you speak today, deliberately slow down and lower your voice
With one of “my 2,” use a gentle tone in place of your usual hurrying or ordering
lessons.noon: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart.” — Lord, right now I learn from you.

lessons.title: Moses, the Humblest of Men
lessons.theme: Those whom God affirms need not rush to defend themselves

v: They said, “Has the LORD indeed spoken only with Moses? Hasn’t he spoken also with us?” And the LORD heard it.
Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.
My servant Moses is not so. He is faithful in all my house.

lessons.still: Remember a time you were misunderstood or criticised. Don’t hurry to defend yourself in your mind; quietly hand it over to the Lord: “Lord, you heard it all.” Let God be your defender; all you need to do is return to him.
teach: A deeply rooted tree doesn’t topple when someone kicks it, nor is it in a hurry to kick back. Miriam and Aaron — Moses’ own sister and brother — publicly challenged his authority. Attacked by those closest to him, Moses did not hit back. Scripture simply inserts one sentence at this point: “Now the man Moses was very humble, above all the men who were on the surface of the earth.”

“And Yahweh heard it.” Moses did not need to defend himself, because God himself stepped in and said, “My servant Moses… is faithful in all my house.” Humility is not having no convictions; it is entrusting your reputation to God. Later, when Miriam was punished, it was Moses who cried out to God to heal her — a gentle person can even intercede for the one who hurt him.

As a young man, Moses killed an Egyptian in a fit of passion — that was self-ruled strength. After forty years in the wilderness, he became “very humble.” Gentleness is refined in us by God. A change of mindset: when I am criticised, I don’t have to rush to prove I am right, because my worth was settled long ago in God.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let people be people and let God be God. Self-ruled people insist on vindicating themselves and guarding their own reputation; people living the self-emptied life return to their place and let God be God. Pride provokes pride: had Moses hit back, the family would have been torn apart. He chose humility, and God himself vindicated him.
q: Who is God? — “And Yahweh heard it” — how have you experienced God as your defender?
Who am I? — When you are misunderstood, is your first reaction to defend yourself, to hit back, or to entrust it to God?
How shall I respond? — What part of your “reputation” do you need to hand over to God’s protection today?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was falsely accused before Pilate, he “gave him no answer, not even one word, so that the governor marveled greatly.” It was not that he had nothing to say; he entrusted himself to the Father, who judges justly. His silence was not weakness but the deepest gentleness and trust.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that when I am misunderstood I am quick to defend myself, and even to strike back. Refine me as you refined Moses, and make me a humble person. I hand my reputation over to you; you are my defender. Help me to pray for those who hurt me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: When you are criticised today, pause for three seconds and pray silently before you respond
Pray for someone who once misunderstood you
When you disagree with one of “my 2,” listen all the way through before rushing to explain yourself
lessons.noon: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” — Lord, right now I leave my defence to you.

lessons.title: The Gentle Shall Inherit the Earth
lessons.theme: Those who do not grab and fight end up receiving God’s inheritance

v: Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth.
But the humble shall inherit the land, and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace.

lessons.still: Think of something you have badly wanted to win lately, or are afraid to lose: a position, some recognition, an opportunity. Slowly open your clenched hand, hold it out before the Lord, and say, “Lord, my inheritance is in your hands.”
teach: The world’s logic says that if you want land, you must be tough — you must fight and grab. Throughout history, land has mostly been won by the sword. Yet Jesus said something that turns this upside down: “Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth.” To “inherit” means to receive as heirs — the inheritance is not seized; it is given by the Father.

Jesus’ words echo Psalm 37. Seeing the wicked prosper, the psalmist urges, “Don’t fret,” but rest quietly and trust in the Lord. The gentle are not blind to injustice; they believe God governs all things, so they don’t need to grab with their own hands. God himself will give the inheritance to his children.

Self-ruled people are afraid of losing out, so they fight; people living the self-emptied life know they are God’s children, so they can give way. Abraham let Lot choose the land first, and afterwards God said to him, “All the land which you see, I will give to you.” A change of mindset: giving way is not losing; in God’s hands, what we yield is what we gain.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A shift in perspective — from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal. The gentle do not rely on seizing but on inheriting, because their focus is on God, not on their circumstances. Humility draws out humility and everyone wins; those who do not fight end up receiving the most.
q: Who is God? — God is the Father who gives an inheritance — how does that change the way you see gain and loss?
Who am I? — In what situation do you fight because you are afraid of losing out?
How shall I respond? — Where can you “give way” a step today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was the heir of all things, yet on earth he had nowhere to lay his head. He did not grasp at an earthly kingdom, yet he received an everlasting one. He was obedient to the point of death, so God highly exalted him, that every knee should bow to him. “The gentle shall inherit the earth” — Jesus is the perfect proof.
lessons.pray: Father, I confess that I am often afraid of losing out and want to grab things with my own hands. Today I open my hands, trusting that my inheritance is in yours. Make me gentle — not fighting, not grabbing, not fretting — at peace to receive everything you give. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: In some small matter, freely let someone else choose first
Write down one thing you are clinging to, and pray it over into God’s hands
For one of “my 2,” give up a choice you had planned to insist on
lessons.noon: “Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth.” — Lord, right now I let go and let you be Lord.

lessons.title: A Gentle Answer Turns Away Wrath
lessons.theme: One gentle word can put out a blaze of anger

v: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.

lessons.still: Recall the last conversation in which you raised your voice. In your mind, “replay” it: what would have happened if you had slowed down and softened? Take a deep breath and ask, “Lord, govern my mouth, and govern my heart.”
teach: An argument is like a game of table tennis: you smash the ball at me, I smash it back, and the rally gets faster and fiercer. But the moment one player stops smashing and simply catches the ball softly, the game slows down. Solomon said, “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.”

James gives three things in order: “swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” We often reverse them: slow to hear, swift to speak, and swift to anger. He goes on, “the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.” We think our anger is defending what is right, but often it is only defending ourselves.

A gentle answer does not mean saying something untrue or flattering people; it means speaking the truth in a gentle tone. The content can be clear while the manner stays soft. Gentle words come from a gentle heart — everything we do flows from the heart, and when the heart is governed by the Holy Spirit, the tongue will be tamed by him too.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. Arguing back from the head brings only trouble; living from the heart by the Spirit brings joy. A gentle answer is a moment of letting Jesus reign.
q: Who is God? — God is “slow to anger” — how has he responded gently to your failures?
Who am I? — With whom are you most likely to be “swift to speak and swift to anger”?
How shall I respond? — The next time there is conflict, how will you “catch the ball”?
lessons.jesus: When a Samaritan village refused to welcome Jesus, James and John wanted to call down fire from heaven to destroy it, but Jesus turned and rebuked his disciples. To the woman caught in adultery he said, “Neither do I condemn you.” His words were full of truth and full of gentleness.
lessons.pray: Lord, govern my mouth and my heart. I want to be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. When anger rises, let the Holy Spirit remind me that the anger of man does not produce your righteousness. Make my words gentle, carrying grace and truth as yours do. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: In every conversation today, listen to the end before you speak
When you feel anger rising, lower your voice and slow down
With one of “my 2,” use gentle words to raise something you would otherwise have scolded them for
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath.” — Lord, right now make my words gentle.

lessons.title: Gentle with My 2
lessons.theme: Restore people with a gentle heart, and bear with them with a gentle heart

v: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love,

lessons.still: Think of one of your 2 who is struggling or has fallen. Don’t judge; first pray quietly for them. Then ask yourself, “Lord, if I were in their place, how would I want to be treated?”
teach: When a doctor sets a bone, the technique must be precise and the touch must be light. Too much force causes further injury; too little, and the bone won’t go back into place. The word Paul uses for “restore” carries the sense of setting a bone or mending a fishing net. This week we have seen Jesus’ gentleness (Day 1), Moses’ humility (Day 2), the gentle inheriting the earth (Day 3), and the gentle answer (Day 4).

Paul says, “You who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” The mark of spirituality is not pointing out faults most accurately but restoring people most gently. He adds a warning: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” Gentleness is rooted in humility — I know I could fall too, so I won’t look down on anyone.

Ephesians links gentleness with humility, patience and love, so that we “bear with one another.” Being gentle with my 2 means remembering that they, like me, are sinners who have received grace. Next week we will learn self-control; gentleness and self-control both belong to a life tamed by the Holy Spirit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The practice of 920 — the “0” of the self-emptied life frees us from putting ourselves at the centre, so we can treat each of our 2 with gentleness. Life first, then relationships, then ministry; winning back a person matters more than winning an argument. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.
q: Who is God? — How has God gently restored you when you fell?
Who am I? — When others fall, are you the doctor setting the bone or the judge pronouncing the verdict?
How shall I respond? — With what kind of gentleness will you restore or bear with which of your 2?
lessons.jesus: After Peter denied him three times, the risen Jesus did not rebuke him. Instead, by the Sea of Galilee he prepared a charcoal fire and breakfast for him, and then asked him three times, “Do you love me?” Three denials were healed by three questions of love. This is what it means to restore someone in a spirit of gentleness.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you once restored me gently. Make me gentle too, so that when brothers and sisters are weak I neither judge nor despise them, but humbly support them. I place my 2 in your hands; use me to be a blessing to them. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Call one of “my 2” to see how they are, or send them a warm message
Pray for someone who is going through a weak time, and ask them what help they need
Tomorrow (Saturday), share this week’s practice of gentleness with your spiritual companion
lessons.noon: “With all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love” — Lord, right now let me treat people with gentleness.

mem.t: Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible.

lessons.title: Self-Control Is the Spirit in Charge
lessons.theme: Self-control is not me holding myself in check, but letting the Holy Spirit govern me

v: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.

lessons.still: Quietly ask: right now, what inside me most wants to take charge? Tiredness, a desire, an emotion, a thought? Acknowledge it without judging it, and then say, “Holy Spirit, please take charge of this place.”
teach: A car’s steering wheel can only be held by one person. Many people understand self-control as “gripping the wheel myself” — gritting their teeth and relying on willpower. But willpower is like a rubber band: the tighter you stretch it, the harder it snaps back. So people who try to control themselves by their own strength often swing back and forth between repression and indulgence.

Self-control is the last of the nine fruits. Paul does not say, “Control yourselves, and you won’t indulge your desires,” but “walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” The key is “by the Spirit.” Those who belong to Christ have already crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts; now we are to “walk by the Spirit.”

So the secret of self-control is not to control ourselves harder but to hand over control more completely. A change of mindset: self-control is not “I keep myself in check” but “the Holy Spirit keeps me in check.” When the Spirit holds the wheel, we stop where we should stop and go where we should go.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. Self-ruled people either indulge themselves or suppress themselves by their own effort — and both are the self on the throne. People living the self-emptied life let the Holy Spirit reign, and that is true freedom. Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself.
q: Who is God? — The Holy Spirit lives in you and is willing to govern every part of you — how does that make you feel?
Who am I? — In which area do you often swing between “repression” and “indulgence”?
How shall I respond? — Which steering wheel will you hand over to the Holy Spirit today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was “led by the Spirit into the wilderness,” and after fasting forty days and nights, the devil told him to turn stones into bread. He had the power to do it, yet he chose not to, and resisted the temptation with the word of God. His self-control was not repression but a life wholly yielded to the Spirit, feeding on the Father’s word.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, I confess that I often want to hold the wheel myself, and I end up either indulging myself or wearing myself out. Today I hand control over to you. Govern my body, my emotions, my desires and my time, so that I walk by you and bear the fruit of self-control. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: In a moment when you want to indulge today, pray silently: “Holy Spirit, please take charge.”
Memorise this week’s verse: 1 Corinthians 9:25
When you feel like losing your temper with one of “my 2,” stop and ask the Holy Spirit to take charge before you speak
lessons.noon: “Walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” — Lord, right now let the Holy Spirit take charge of me.

lessons.title: Paul Disciplines His Body
lessons.theme: For an incorruptible crown, we gladly train ourselves

v: I therefore run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air,
but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be disqualified.

lessons.still: Sit up straight with your feet on the floor, and become aware of your body. This body is a temple of the Holy Spirit. Say to the Lord, “Lord, my body is yours.” Then consider: whom is my body serving today — my desires, or my Lord?
teach: For the sake of a medal, athletes will rise early for years, control their diet and train every day. They don’t hate good food; they simply have a bigger goal. Paul says that those who compete “exercise self-control in all things,” only to receive “a corruptible crown” — in the ancient games, the victor’s crown was woven from leaves and withered within days.

Paul says, “I run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air.” A person with self-control has a sense of direction. He goes on, “I beat my body and bring it into submission.” My body does not lead me around; I lead my body. The word translated “beat” is a boxing term, describing a resolve not to give in to the flesh.

But this is not asceticism. Paul disciplined his body not to earn salvation but because he valued his witness to the gospel, lest he fail to live out what he preached to others. Self-control is training motivated by grace: because I am already loved, I am willing to live for the crown that cannot perish.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A shift in perspective — from the temporary to the eternal. Self-ruled people live for immediate gratification; people living the self-emptied life live for an eternal crown. Self-control is not losing enjoyment but gaining a greater glory — letting Jesus receive all the glory.
q: Who is God? — God has prepared “an incorruptible crown” for you — what hope does that give you?
Who am I? — Is your life like “beating the air,” or does it have a clear direction?
How shall I respond? — In which bodily habit will you practise self-control today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “withdrew himself into the desert, and prayed,” and often rose before dawn to pray. His body grew tired and hungry too, yet it always remained under the Father’s will. For the joy set before him, he laid down his own will in Gethsemane and walked to the cross.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for preparing an incorruptible crown for me. Help me not to run aimlessly but to live for you. I offer my body to you; Holy Spirit, help me to discipline it — not to earn your love, but because you already love me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Choose one bodily habit (sleep, eating, or your phone) and practise discipline in it for a whole week
Go to bed on time tonight, preparing your body for tomorrow morning’s devotions
Share your training goal with one of “my 2” and ask them to pray for you
lessons.noon: “I beat my body and bring it into submission.” — Lord, right now my body submits to your will.

lessons.title: Self-Control of the Tongue
lessons.theme: Whoever can bridle the tongue can bridle the whole body

v: For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.
Set a watch, LORD, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.

lessons.still: Close your mouth and be silent for a minute. Say nothing, and set aside even the talking inside your head. Then softly pray, “Set a watch, Lord, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.”
